items.title: 🎃 The Real Nightmare Isn't a Bug. It's a Bug Nobody Notices. 🎃
items.summary: Imagine deploying a new feature. All tests pass. CI is green. No errors in the logs. Everything looks fine. Then a user reports that their payment was processed twice. Here's a simplified example of what can go wrong: async function processPayment(order) { try { return await paymentAPI.charge({ amount: order.total, customerId: order.customerId }); } catch (error) { if (error.code === "TIMEOUT") { return await paymentAPI.charge({ amount: order.total, customerId: order.customerId }); } throw error; } } Looks reasonable, but there's a problem. The first request might have reached the payment service and completed successfully. Only the response got lost. The retry sends another charge request. Now imagine this happening with a real customer. One way to prevent this is to use an idempotency key: async function processPayment(order) { return await paymentAPI.charge({ amount: order.total, customerId: order.customerId, idempotencyKey: `payment-${order.id}` }); } Now the payment service can recognize repeated requests for the same operation and return the original result instead of charging the customer again. items.summary: You change one line in the checkout code, a discount that should only apply above fifty dollars, and now you need to know whether anything else broke. The honest answer is that you do not know, and guessing costs more than checking. Running the shop by hand means adding items to the cart, applying the code, and doing the maths yourself, every single time you change anything. A test runner takes that job over. Vitest watches your files, reruns the checks the moment you save, and tells you in under a second whether the totals still add up. This post sets it up on a small shop cart, breaks one test on purpose, and fixes it. My judgement is that Vitest is the right default when the project already runs on Vite, and a good choice for most new JavaScript and TypeScript projects besides. If your front end builds with Vite, Vitest reuses the same config, the same plugins, and the same module handling, so setup is quick. Its test API will also feel familiar if you have used Jest: describe, test, and expect work the way you would guess, so the team learns the runner, not a new dialect. items.title: gRPC Explained: APIs That Speak in Binary
items.summary: A shop dashboard needs one thing from the orders service: the details of order 1042. Over plain JSON the request is easy to write and easy to break. A field is renamed from customer_name to customerName, the dashboard still reads the old name, and the page shows a blank. Nothing errors, and it surfaces only when a customer asks where their parcel is. Server and client each hold a private idea of what an order looks like, and nothing checks that the two still match. gRPC closes exactly that gap: both sides share one contract, a .proto file, and the code on each side is generated from it, so a renamed field breaks the build instead of the page. A gRPC service starts with a contract, not with code. The contract is a .proto file that names the service, its methods, and the shape of every message, using Protocol Buffers, a binary format. A tool reads that file and generates the client and server code in your language, so both sides agree on the shape of the data by construction. The calls travel over HTTP/2, which lets many calls share one connection, and the messages travel as compact binary instead of text, so they are smaller and faster to parse than JSON. gRPC also supports streamin

items.title: WebSockets Explained: Real-Time Data Without Polling
items.summary: A customer adds a ceramic mug to their basket on a small shop's website, then waits. The order page says Processing, and nothing changes until they refresh. The server knew the order shipped ten minutes ago, but the page had no way of hearing about it. The usual fix is polling: the page asks the server "anything new?" every few seconds. Most of those requests get the answer "no", yet each one opens and closes a connection for nothing. WebSockets exist for exactly this gap. One connection stays open, the server pushes a message the moment something changes, and the page updates without asking again. The question is whether your page needs a live wire at all. A WebSocket starts as an ordinary HTTP request that asks the server to upgrade the connection. If the server agrees, that same connection stays open for two-way messages, and either side can send at any time. That is the whole idea. The rest of this post is about deciding when that open connection earns its keep, and what breaks when you treat it like a normal request. items.title: Node.js Webhook Retries: Delayed Queues and Replaceable Recovery Boundaries
items.summary: If a weekly media digest webhook fails, retry the delivery outside the request handler. Put the task in a delayed queue, record the attempt and payload identity, and make the worker’s acknowledgement decision explicit. The application should own that small contract. The queue provider should be replaceable behind it. Short answer: use a delayed queue with exponential backoff, stable task IDs, and explicit ACK/NACK handling; choose the provider whose recovery boundary matches your operations, then hide it behind a small Node.js adapter. That shape gives you operational recovery without tying the digest code to one queue API. A failed delivery can be retried with backoff, moved to a dead-letter path after a policy limit, and inspected with enough history to answer a very practical question: what happened to this customer’s digest? items.title: A search box needed titles. The page sent 300 full records, 41,000 characters of meta descriptions.
items.summary: A single search box on one home page was backed by 255,881 characters of serialized records. The box matches on titles. 106,706 of those characters were fields it can never display. I crawled the home page of 114 sites in one content network, captured the raw HTML before any JavaScript ran, and measured how much of that HTML was Next.js App Router's inline Flight payload — the self.__next_f.push(...) calls that carry the React Server Component tree to the client. 30 of the 114 sites ran App Router. Across those 30 home pages, 48.2% of the combined HTML was Flight payload, and 3.5% was visible text. For comparison, the 84 sites that shipped plain server-rendered HTML landed at 16.5% visible text. That gap is the whole story, and it has two different causes. Both are measurable, and both are fixable without abandoning the framework. No headless browser, no Lighthouse. Just urllib and a regex against the raw response, so every number below can be reproduced by anyone with curl. The Flight payload in an App Router HTML response arrives as a series of calls: self.__next_f.push([1,"1:\"$Sreact.fragment\"\n2:I[35176,[\"/_next/static/chunks/…\"],\"\"]\n…"]) Each argument is a JSON string.

items.title: Day 14: Extension Points on a Business Object and When to Override Them
items.summary: Behavior a definition can express needs no code written at all. The ones it cannot express are what needs taking over: what to check before this document is submitted, who to notify after it is saved, and under what circumstances a delete is not allowed. The way the framework offers to take over is inheriting from a business object and overriding a few of its steps. A subclass adds this form's own logic at the matching step as required, and the hard part is judging which step is the matching one, and whether that code belongs before or after base. A method name can only answer the order, with DoBeforeSave before the save and DoAfterSave after it. The rest has to be stated by the framework. items.title: How I built a Wordle-style daily puzzle in SwiftUI (no backend)
items.summary: I recently shipped Gemdoku: Daily Block Puzzle, a 9×9 block puzzle for iPhone. The core feature is a Wordle-style Daily Challenge: every player in the world gets the same goal, the same move limit and the exact same sequence of pieces each day. It turned out to be a fun little engineering problem. Here's how it works under the hood, all in plain Swift and SwiftUI, with no backend. The obvious way to give everyone the same puzzle is to generate it on a server. I didn't want a backend. The game is fully offline, has no accounts and collects no data. So the daily puzzle has to be derived, not downloaded. The trick is a seeded random number generator. Swift's RandomNumberGenerator protocol makes this easy. items.title: Container Queries and Focus Management: Building Resilient Components with TailwindCSS v4
items.summary: Container Queries and Focus Management: Building Resilient Components with TailwindCSS v4 When integrating meta/astryx into a production TypeScript stack last quarter, we hit a painful wall: our card components looked pristine in desktop viewports but collapsed into unusable layouts when nested inside sidebars or widget containers. The root cause wasn't the design system itself—it was our reliance on viewport-based media queries instead of container queries. Combined with improperly managed focus trapping in modal overlays, our accessibility score tanked. Let's walk through the hard-won fixes. Viewport-based breakpoints assume a global coordinate system. When meta/astryx components lived inside a max-w-xs sidebar, our md: and lg: classes fired anyway, rendering a responsive grid that had no space to breathe. According to Cord Cutters News, the creator pulled the license after Roku's sale to FOX was announced. Ars Technica reports: The screensaver has been an option for Roku OS users for 10 years. Roku has been licensing the animation, which is called the Marine Aquarium, from artist Jim Sachs through Prolific Publishing. Sachs is the creator and copyright holder of the Marine Aquarium. He developed the screensaver through his company SereneScreen. He tells Ars Technica that the licensing agreement with Roku is up for renewal every October and can be canceled by either party for any reason. A day after learning that Fox was planning to buy Roku, a deal that closed today, Sachs told Prolific that he wouldn't be renewing Roku's license. "I can't be part of the Fox world," he tells Ars, pointing to Fox News' controversial style of news and entertainment. items.title: Six React chart libraries against hand-written SVG: what I found
items.summary: I worked on an analytics product with about sixteen charts: survival curves, forest plots, histograms and scatter plots. Our charting library had not published a release in over a year. Nothing was broken, but I was worried about future React upgrades and who would maintain it. I wanted to know what we could move to. I took two charts from the product, a survival curve and a scatter plot, and built each with nivo, Recharts, ECharts, visx, TanStack Charts and Chart.js. I also built them in React with hand-written SVG. All seven implementations followed the same spec and used the same synthetic data, with animation off. At typical sizes (three survival series with 200 points each, and a 500-point scatter) the native-speed timings gave me no clear winner. Within each chart type, all seven were less than one frame apart. At 10,000 scatter points, the median mount times spread out: 24 ms for hand-written SVG, 33 ms for visx, 53 ms for TanStack Charts, 80–86 ms for Chart.js and ECharts, 310 ms for Recharts and 3.2 seconds for nivo's SVG scatter. items.title: React Async States That Keep Forms Honest
items.summary: Forms are where a polished product can suddenly feel unreliable. A user submits an email, the button spins, and then… nothing useful happens. Maybe the request is still running. Maybe the server rejected the address. Maybe the response succeeded but the UI forgot to move on. In React, this often starts with a harmless-looking isLoading boolean. Over time it becomes a bucket for validation, network work, success messages, retries, and failures. The component still works, but it is hard to explain and harder to recover. The better approach is to give the form a small, explicit async state model. It makes the JavaScript easier to reason about, and it gives users a clearer product experience. Consider this common shape: const [isLoading, setIsLoading] = useState(false); const [error, setError] = useState(null); It looks simple until you ask a few questions: Should a second submit be blocked while client validation runs? Can the user edit the field after a server error? Does an old response still have permission to overwrite a newer attempt? What should the button say after success? items.title: I built a live mess-menu app for my university — here's the stack and why it stuck
items.summary: Every hostel student at my university wakes up to the same question: what's the mess serving, and is it worth walking down for? The "official" answer was a PDF that nobody kept up to date. This week — the full weekly menu so you can plan around the good days. Ratings & reviews — students rate each meal, so "chicken karahi" with a 4.5 reads very differently from one with a 1.8. No login. No ads. Free. Deliberately boring, because boring is reliable: React + TypeScript on the frontend. items.title: Hangfire Alternative in .NET: Why I Replaced It With BackgroundService and Channel
items.summary: The first version of this site was an ASP.NET Core MVC app with Hangfire wired in: a dashboard at /hangfire, five recurring jobs, ten places in the code that called BackgroundJob.Enqueue, and a second SQL Server database just to hold Hangfire's job tables. When I rewrote the backend as a separate Web API, I didn't bring Hangfire with me. The API that serves this page runs two BackgroundService classes fed by System.Threading.Channels, and one WHERE clause does the work of the every-minute job. This isn't a "Hangfire is bad" post. Hangfire is a good library. It's a post about checking which jobs actually needed it, because for this site the answer was none of them. The short version: Use Hangfire (or Quartz.NET) when a job must survive a restart, retry on its own, or be visible on a dashboard. If the work is in-process, short-lived and fine to lose on a crash, a BackgroundService with a bounded Channel is built into .NET, needs no extra database, and is about 60 lines. A job that only "flips something on at a certain time" often needs no job at all: filter by time in the query. items.title: Prevent Spoofed Orders in Next.js Telegram Mini Apps using Server-Validated MainButton Checkout
items.summary: Shipping an e-commerce storefront inside a Telegram Mini App using Next.js App Router seems straightforward until untrusted client state compromises your checkout process. Front-end developers frequently rely on window.Telegram.WebApp.initDataUnsafe to identify the user and send cart totals directly from the client to an API route. Because initDataUnsafe can be mutated by anyone opening your app in a standard browser or using browser developer tools, accepting unverified user IDs or total prices from the front end allows users to modify invoice amounts, impersonate other customer accounts, or execute unverified orders. Building a robust Telegram Mini App shop requires verifying the raw initData payload using an HMAC-SHA256 signature on the server, calculating cart prices strictly from stored backend database values, controlling Telegram's native MainButton across React render lifecycles, and accounting for renderer discrepancies between iOS WebViews and Telegram Desktop. items.title: Domain exceptions between NestJS and React: an identifier with data, not a sentence
items.summary: This is how the client of this API dispatches a shipment: // client/src/modules/shipment/services/dispatch-shipment.ts import { instance } from "@modules/app/modules/http/domain/instance"; import { DispatchShipmentDTO } from "../dto/write/dispatch-shipment"; export async function dispatchShipment( props: DispatchShipmentDTO, ): Promise { try { await instance.post("/shipments/dispatch", props); return true; } catch { return false; } } And this is how it is consumed, in the button component: // client/src/modules/shipment/components/DispatchButton/hooks/useDispatchButton.tsx const dispatched = await dispatchShipment({ shipmentId, carrierId }); if (!dispatched) { toastError({ en: "The shipment could not be dispatched.", es: "No se pudo despachar el envío.", }); } This code is not a bug, and reviewed on its own there is nothing to fix. The parameterless catch is not even carelessness: it is the honest way of saying "this can fail and I am not going to make up why". items.title: Britain to Make Salary Disclosure In Job Ads Mandatory
items.summary: Britain plans to require employers to disclose salaries in job advertisements. "Whether you're a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it," Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a statement. Reuters reports: The government said requiring companies to disclose pay in job ads would help young people applying for their first jobs, while boosting pay transparency and helping tackle disparities that can disadvantage women. Just over two in five employers always publish salary ranges, while fewer than one in five always disclose specific salaries, Burnham's office said, citing estimates from the Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development. The government will soon introduce legislation to parliament making salary disclosures mandatory, Burnham's office said, although it did not provide a timeline. Nearly one million, or 13%, of 16 to 24 year-olds in Britain are not in employment, education or training, one of the highest shares in Europe. A government review into youth inactivity is due to be published later in November. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: When “Working as Designed” Is the Problem
items.summary: I submitted a security report to Anthropic after Claude Code exposed my .NET User Secrets in its model context. They classified it as “Informative – Working as Designed.” “Working as designed” is a triage label, not a verdict. But taken at face value, it points to something architectural: security is enforced tool by tool, not around the agent as a whole, and certainly not at the OS-boundary level. .NET developers commonly use dotnet user-secrets to keep development credentials in their user profile, outside the project tree. These secrets can include: • API keys • Database connection strings • Passwords • Third-party service credentials • Other sensitive application configuration Consider this scenario: You have a .NET application. You have configured User Secrets. You launch Claude Code in your project directory. You ask Claude to inspect your application configuration. Claude can execute: dotnet user-secrets list And/or read the plaintext secrets.json file. %APPDATA%\Microsoft\UserSecrets\ \secrets.json Because tool output is returned to Claude, those credentials become part of the conversation context. items.title: Permission-heavy multi-tenant systems: make the access check boring
items.summary: Permission-heavy systems become risky when access rules are scattered across controllers, UI checks, repository filters, and background jobs. The aim is not a clever authorization framework. It is one rule path that is difficult to bypass. The examples come from Shield, Zotic, CAS, Question Banking and Amlaak. Every protected operation can be described with four values: the actor, the tenant, the action, and the resource. If one is unknown, the system does not yet have enough information to allow the operation. This simple tuple prevents a common mistake: checking that a user has a permission somewhere, then loading a resource that belongs to another tenant. Permission and ownership need to be evaluated together. The decision input public sealed record AccessRequest( Guid ActorId, Guid TenantId, string Action, string ResourceType, Guid? ResourceId); A route parameter or request body can name a tenant, but it cannot prove membership in that tenant. Resolve the active tenant from authenticated membership, then compare any requested tenant identifier with it. items.title: Building a service status notifier with .NET and Cloudflare Workers
items.summary: I've been working on a small side project recently. Like most developers I depend on quite a few external services. GitHub, Cloudflare, OpenAI, and others. When something breaks, I usually end up checking their individual status pages to figure out what's going on. I wanted a simpler way to keep track of these incidents and get notified in Slack without having to configure every provider separately. So I started building StatusRelay. Why build another status monitoring tool? Of course, tools like this already exist, and they offer much more comprehensive solutions. I wasn't trying to reinvent everything they do. I just wanted something lightweight where I could select the services I care about, connect a Slack channel or webhook, and start receiving notifications. No accounts, no paid plans, and no complicated setup. It also seemed like a fun opportunity to experiment with event processing, background jobs, and reliable notification delivery. But how does it work?! The idea is pretty straightforward: Poll official status APIs from different providers. Normalize their status and incident information. Store incidents and detect changes. Send notifications to Slack or custom webhooks.

items.title: I Stamped Every Row With DateTime.Now and Paid Twice
items.summary: I had a batch importer stamping DateTime.Now onto every row it processed. A few hundred thousand rows, one timestamp each, nothing I'd ever think twice about. Then I put a profiler on the thing because it was slower than it had any right to be, and there it was near the top: reading the clock. Not the database, not the parsing. The clock. So I did the thing I always end up doing. I counted. DateTime.Now doesn't read a "local clock." There's no such thing. It reads UTC, exactly like DateTime.UtcNow does, and then converts that instant into local time using TimeZoneInfo.Local. That conversion is the whole difference between the two calls. One reads the clock. The other reads the clock and then asks the time zone database what your offset is right now, DST and all. The offset lookup is the part that costs. And here's the bit that surprised me: it costs even when the answer is zero. I read each one 20 million times, summed the ticks so nothing got optimized away, best of five rounds. items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Scientific American: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch, an area in the Pacific Ocean where debris naturally accumulates, is full of tiny bits of plastic -- so full, in fact, that it seems to be changing the color of the ocean. [...] To better understand how microplastics may have influenced the ocean's color, [Daniel Koestner, a postdoctoral fellow at the University of Bergen in Norway] and his colleagues looked at 20 years of satellite data from the spot in the ocean with perhaps the most of plastic -- the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, a zone between Hawaii and California where trash trapped by ocean currents accumulates. Between 2002 and 2022, the researchers found, waters near the garbage patch have gotten brighter in both blue and green wavelengths compared with surrounding areas. The results, published in the journal Communications Earth & Environment on Thursday, don't yet prove that microplastics have directly brightened the ocean, the researchers emphasize, though their findings are backed up by lab experiments with microplastics. items.title: They Created a Cell That's Almost Alive. What to Do With It Now? (8 minute read)
items.summary: A SpudCell is an artificial cell created from lifeless ingredients that can grow, copy its DNA, divide in two, and start its cell cycle all over again. It is still far from a self-sustaining cell that any scientist could manufacture from prepared ingredients, but the technology could eventually make it easier to produce medicines, foods, and other items that could not otherwise be produced with ordinary biology. The researchers working on SpudCell hope that it will eventually be a platform for biotechnology that will allow a simple cell to be engineered in scores of useful ways. SpudCell could potentially be misused, so its researchers are taking security seriously from the start - its DNA and proteins are engineered so that it can only survive on an exotic diet of chemicals not found in nature.

items.title: OpenAI Responds to US Midterm Elections With New Commitment to Communities
items.summary: "OpenAI has published a new National Community Compact and Compute Campus Policy Blueprint, apparently in response to the Blue Wave Midterm Elections," writes ancient Slashdot reader Gilmoure. "Instead of moving into communities like a juggernaut, they say they will be dangling friendly carrots going forward." Here's an excerpt from OpenAI's article: Every future compute campus OpenAI owns and operates will have its own local compact. We'll engage residents early enough to ensure their input shapes project plans, give them a local point of contact throughout the life of the campus, and report publicly each year on how we're doing. Each compact will reflect local priorities and include a common set of commitments: - Pay our own way on energy and infrastructure. We'll pay the full cost of the electricity we use and the infrastructure needed to serve us. Before major spending begins, we'll provide financial assurances so other customers are protected if a project is delayed, reduced, or canceled. - Protect local resources and report on our impact. We'll develop a water plan for each campus, prioritize closed-loop or low-water cooling, and publish site-level water and electricity use.

items.title: Mining 14,351 Chess Puzzles with Stockfish 18 (and the Illegal-FEN Trap in chess.js)
items.summary: When we started building Brass Pawn (source on GitHub, AGPLv3), we needed a large offline tactics, positional judgement, and endgame dataset that ran completely on-device—both in the browser and natively on iPhone, iPad, and Mac. Transcribing chess puzzles by hand or scraping unverified problem collections breaks down fast. Two failure modes show up immediately in real training: Cooked solutions: A position has a flashy sacrifice, so a human annotator marks it as winning—missing a quiet defensive resource at depth 18, or missing a second equally winning move that punishes a student for playing an objectively strong alternative. Horizon flips: A shallow engine pass (depth 10–12) flags a move as +2.10, only for depth 22 to reveal perpetual check (0.00). Instead of transcribing puzzles, we built a deterministic mining and independent verification pipeline powered by Stockfish 18. Along the way, we hit a subtle FEN validation edge case in chess.js that silently breaks UCI engines. A good tactics puzzle isn't simply "someone blundered in a game." items.title: Making a SwiftUI app survive a folding iPhone: what broke on the iPhone Duo and how I fixed it
items.summary: I make PawLife, a small pet health app (feeding plans in grams, a health diary, a food safety lookup). It is one SwiftUI codebase for iPhone, iPad, Mac Catalyst, Apple Watch and visionOS. When Xcode 27.2 shipped simulators for the iPhone Duo, I expected "it is just a wider iPhone". It is not. Here is what actually broke, in the order I found it, and what the fixes looked like. The Duo has an outer display and an inner one across the fold. Your app runs on one of them at a time, and the window changes size when the user folds or unfolds. The simulator reports it as a window resize, not a new scene. Measured on the simulator: Folded: a 466×678 pt window, of which my app got 382 pt of width. The remaining 84 pt on the trailing edge is a reserved column (status area and camera) exposed through the safe area. Open: a landscape 951×669 pt window, 867 pt for the app, with the same 84 pt trailing column. So the app goes from a narrow portrait phone to a wide landscape slab and back, live, without a relaunch. items.title: iOS silent push not working: content-available and background pushes
items.summary: A silent push, which Apple calls a background notification, has no alert, sound or badge. It wakes your app so it can fetch new content. Apple treats it as low priority and does not guarantee delivery, so "it worked once and then stopped" is often the system working as designed. This page goes through what must be right on the sender and in the app, and what the device itself decides. What you see Likely cause Fix Never arrives, alert pushes work Remote notifications background mode not ticked Signing and Capabilities > Background Modes > Remote notification Shows a banner instead of waking the app quietly alert, sound or badge in aps next to content-available Send aps with content-available: 1 and nothing else APNs returns 400 apns-priority: 10 with apns-push-type: background Priority 5 for background pushes, always Delivered late, or in bursts Priority 5 pushes are sent according to the device's power state Expected; use an alert push for anything a person waits for Arrives in testing, then stops Throttled: too many background pushes Two or three an hour at most Nothing after the user swiped the app away The app was force quit Nothing to fix; it wakes again once the user opens it

items.title: Understanding SwiftUI's layoutPriority: HStack, ZStack, and Custom Layouts
items.summary: SwiftUI makes building interfaces straightforward, but its layout system can sometimes produce unexpected results. One modifier that developers often reach for is .layoutPriority(). For example: swift This can help resolve layout issues, but what exactly does the priority value mean? And does the modifier behave the same way in every container? To explore these questions, I built an interactive open-source project called SwiftUI Layout Lab. The .layoutPriority() modifier provides a priority value that parent layouts can use when determining how to size their children. The default priority is 0. A higher priority doesn't directly specify a width, height, or percentage of available space. Its effect depends on the parent layout algorithm and the sizing behavior of the child views. For example, assigning a priority of 100 doesn't mean a view will receive 100 times more space than a view with priority 1. An HStack arranges views horizontally, but what happens when there isn't enough space for every view to receive its preferred width? In Layout Lab, you can: Select one of three views. Change its layout priority. Adjust the available container width. Observe the actual measured widths.

items.title: Swift. AppKit. No Electron. Coding agents in a native Mac app
items.summary: Swift. AppKit. No Electron. I built Coincide as a native Mac app for the coding agents I already use. Here is a new 10-second motion preview: A Mac interface built with Swift and AppKit Coincide's main interface is built with AppKit, with SwiftUI where it fits, such as Settings. It brings native menus, Mac keyboard shortcuts, a native transcript and the agent/model picker into one window. The clip calls out the architecture: Swift. AppKit. No Electron. That describes Coincide's Mac interface. It isn't a benchmark or a claim that every workload is faster than another app. Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode and Antigravity each run through their own command-line tool and existing login. Coincide does not sell or meter tokens. When you switch agents mid-thread, the next agent gets a recap of the turns it missed and works in the same directory. Each agent keeps its own native session. Switching back resumes that agent's session. The handoff deep dive covers the mechanism and its limits. The preview browses Codex, Claude Code and Cursor's picker catalogs. Available models depend on the agents installed and the provider account you use. This is an edited illustrative demo:

items.title: Crop Once, Post Everywhere: Batch Aspect-Ratio Crops for Social Images in Swift
items.summary: If you ship photos from an iPhone app to more than one place, you eventually hit the same boring problem: Instagram wants 1:1 or 4:5, a shop banner wants 16:9, Stories want 9:16, and the camera roll is full of 4:3 and 3:4 stills. Doing that crop by hand for thirty product shots is how afternoons disappear. This post walks through a small UIKit pipeline that takes one UIImage, a list of target aspect ratios, and returns one centre-weighted crop per ratio — suitable for running across a whole album. I’m writing it from the seat of someone who builds BatchMark, an on-device batch photo app, where “apply the same finishing step to many photos” is the whole product. The code below is a teaching extract, not a dump of the app. People say “crop to 1:1” and mean two different things: Aspect-fill crop: keep the photo’s resolution as high as possible, cut off the edges that don’t fit the ratio. Aspect-fit pad: show the whole photo, add bars (or a mat) to reach the ratio. For social uploads you almost always want (1). items.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time review – a dream come true
items.summary: Nintendo Switch 2; Nintendo This ambitious remake transforms a landmark Zelda game into a modern masterpiece, clearer and easier to navigate, more beautiful to look at, with playful musical touches. Yet the melancholy remains It’s always a worry, returning to a formative piece of art from your childhood. Will your jaded adult sensibilities render you unable to locate the magic that captivated your child self? Will revisiting it reveal that it was never actually that good, and that your tastes are built on a foundation of lies? With video games, there is the added complication of technological advancement: decades-old games can look so basic and feel so treacly to play that it’s hard to explain why they were mind-blowing at the time. Light-touch remasters aim to bring such games up to modern graphical standards without fundamentally changing them; an ambitious remake attempts to transform the work into something that can stand alongside any modern masterpiece. Ocarina of Time is the latter. And I could not be more delighted to report that it is a dream come true. Continue reading...

Then he might check in with Betsy for search engine optimization, or Juno for onboarding customers. items.title: Is a job guarantee the solution to mass AI unemployment?
items.summary: An old idea springs anew as a chorus of influential voices predicts that AI may trigger crises of vast magnitude In a preface to his book Capitalism and Freedom, the American economist Milton Friedman famously observed that a crisis can propel once-fringe ideas into the political mainstream. “Only a crisis – actual or perceived – produces real change. When that crisis occurs, the actions that are taken depend on the ideas that are lying around,” he wrote. The job of intellectuals, thinktanks and economists, he argued, is to refine the quality of these ambient ideas, so that good ones are ready when disaster strikes. Continue reading...

items.title: ‘The tech bro fight club is real!’ The titans of AI get the Succession treatment in a wild new TV show
items.summary: The Audacity is a fearless satire taking on Silicon Valley’s ‘egomaniac weirdos’. Its creator and stars talk ayahuasca ceremonies, mining kids for data – and punching CEOs Showrunner Jonathan Glatzer wanted the tagline of his latest TV creation to be: “We’re so fucked.” He laughs. “Sadly it got rejected by the network. Hey, maybe I can use it for season two!” The show in question is The Audacity, his darkly comic drama about AI tech titans. Instead, it went with the more PG tagline “Move fast and break people” – a twist on “Move fast and break things”, the Facebook motto coined by Mark Zuckerberg. The Audacity promises to do for tech bros what Succession did for legacy media. Considering Glatzer is a former writer on Succession, that is no empty threat. This acerbic and all-too-timely Silicon Valley satire follows CEO Duncan Park (played by Billy Magnussen), the obscenely wealthy founder of a data analytics company. items.title: I’m a CTO. AI still needs your human expertise | Madhu Shashanka
items.summary: AI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgment Autonomous cars, which may be the safest we have built, keep getting easily avoidable parking tickets. While Waymos crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions of miles, they’re still terrible at performing basic tasks – keeping out of disabled parking spots and tow-away zones, or steering clear of a church garage during Sunday service, according to the Wall Street Journal. That is the state of AI today: impressively capable at something complex, yet embarrassingly clumsy at something easy. And it has implications for what work will remain human and what will be automated by AI. Madhu Shashanka is co-founder, chief scientist and chief technology officer at Concentric AI, a data security software company Continue reading...
